plumber.intro: Learn plumbing from pipework to water systems. Install, repair, and maintain the systems that bring clean water into buildings and take waste out.

skillDomains.name: Pipework
skillDomains.description: Cut, join, and route pipes for water supply and drainage.

skills.name: Pipe Materials
skills.description: Know which pipe for which job.

modules.title: The pipes you'll work with
modules.content:
PVC (polyvinyl chloride)

Rigid plastic. Cheap, easy to work with, chemical resistant. Common for drainage and cold water supply.

PPR (polypropylene random copolymer)

Heat-resistant plastic. Used for hot water supply. Joined by heat fusion.

Copper

Traditional, durable, expensive. Excellent for hot and cold water.

Galvanised steel

Old installations. Rusts from inside out.

PEX

Flexible plastic. Growing in popularity. Easy to route around obstacles.

steps.q: You're installing a hot water line from the heater to the shower. Which pipe?
You're running a drain line under a house. Which pipe?
steps.f: PVC is the standard for drainage.

steps.q: A client's old house has rusty water from the taps. Likely pipe material?
steps.f: Galvanised steel rusts internally over decades.

skills.name: Joints & Fittings
skills.description: The connections that hold a water system together.

modules.title: Joining pipes
modules.content:
PVC joints

Solvent cement (glue). Clean both surfaces, apply cement, push together, hold 30 seconds, cure 24 hours before pressure testing.

PPR joints

Heat fusion. A special tool melts both pipe and fitting, then they're pushed together and cool into a single piece.

Copper joints

Soldered (sweated) or compression fittings. Soldering requires a torch, flux, and skill.

Threaded joints

Used on galvanised and some brass fittings. Wrap with Teflon tape or hemp before tightening.

steps.q: You're gluing two PVC pipes together. How long before pressure testing?
steps.f: Solvent cement needs 24 hours to fully cure.

steps.q: A threaded joint keeps leaking after tightening. What do you do?
o: Remove, re-apply Teflon tape, and re-tighten

steps.q: Which joint is strongest for hot water?
steps.f: Heat fusion creates a single piece of material.

modules.title: Build a joint sample board
modules.prompt: Create physical samples of at least 5 different pipe joints (PVC glued, PPR fused, copper soldered, threaded, compression). Mount them on a board with labels.
steps: Cut pipe sections for each joint type
Mount on a board with the joint name and pipe material

skillDomains.name: Water Systems
skillDomains.description: The bigger picture — supply, drainage, and pressure.

skills.name: Supply Systems
skills.description: Getting water from the source to the tap.

modules.title: How water gets to a tap
modules.content:
The supply chain

  1. Source — municipal main, borehole, tank, or well
  2. Storage — tank, overhead tank, or cistern
  3. Pump — moves water if gravity isn't enough
  4. Distribution — pipes to each tap
  5. Pressure — provided by gravity (tank height) or a booster pump

Rule of thumb

Water pressure from gravity equals 0.1 bar per metre of height. A tank 10m above a tap provides 1 bar — adequate for household use. A tank on the ground needs a pump.

steps.q: A client wants water to flow from an overhead tank to a ground-floor tap. Tank is 8m above the tap. Will it work?
o: Yes, adequate pressure for household use
Only if the pipe is thin
steps.f: 8m of head ≈ 0.8 bar. Enough for taps and showers.

steps.q: Water pressure is weak at the top floor of a 3-story building. What do you check?
steps.f: Check if the tank is high enough AND whether pipes to the top floor are adequately sized.

steps.q: Which is more reliable for a borehole system: gravity tank or pressure tank?
o: Gravity tank (simpler, no power needed for delivery)
steps.f: Gravity works even when power is out.

modules.title: Drainage principles
modules.content:
Gravity does the work

Drainage relies on slope. Water flows downhill. Fall for standard drainpipes: 1:60 to 1:80 (1cm drop per 60-80cm of pipe).

Ventilation

Drains need air to flow properly. Every drainage system needs a vent pipe running up to the roof (or a one-way air admittance valve). Without it, water in the trap gets sucked out and sewer gases enter the house.

Traps

A U-bend (trap) under every fixture holds a small amount of water that seals against sewer gases. Never install a fixture without a trap.

Access

Every drainage system needs a cleanout point.

steps.q: You're installing a drain for a kitchen sink. What slope is correct?
steps.f: Gentle slope lets solids travel with water.

steps.q: A client complains of bad sewer smell in the bathroom. What's the first thing to check?
o: The trap under the sink — it may be dry or missing
steps.f: Dry or missing traps let sewer gas in.

steps.q: A drain line has no vent. What problem does this cause?
o: Slow drainage and sewer smell (traps get sucked dry)
steps.f: Without venting, water in the trap gets siphoned out.

skillDomains.name: Fault Finding
skillDomains.description: Diagnose leaks, blockages, and low pressure.

skills.name: Leak Detection
skills.description: Find the leak without pulling the whole house apart.

modules.title: Types of leaks
modules.content:
Visible leaks

Water dripping from a joint or fitting. Easy to find and fix.

Hidden leaks

Inside walls, under floors, or underground. Signs include:

  • Water bill higher than normal
  • Damp patches on walls or floors
  • Musty smell
  • Sound of running water with all taps closed
  • Mould growth

The meter test

Turn off all taps and appliances. Check the water meter. If it's still moving, you have a leak.

steps.q: Water bill doubles but no visible leak. What do you do?
o: Meter test with all taps off, then check hidden areas
steps.f: The meter test confirms a leak exists.

steps.q: A damp patch grows on a ceiling below a bathroom. Where's the leak?
o: Above — check the bathroom floor, toilet seal, or drain

steps.q: You hear running water with all taps closed. What does this mean?
o: A leak somewhere in the system
steps.f: Running water with no taps open is either a leak or a running toilet fill valve.

modules.title: What a plumbing quote covers
modules.content:
1. Materials — pipes, fittings, seals, fixtures
  2. Labour — hours × your rate
  3. Overhead — transport, tool wear, insurance
  4. Contingency — 10-15% for surprises behind walls
  5. Margin — 25-40%

The wall problem

You don't know what's behind a wall until you open it. Always warn the client that final cost may increase if hidden conditions are worse than expected.
